article_text:
The Artnet Bulletin is our daily digest of five items from around the art world that are worth knowing. A different writer takes over each morning.

A Personal Note Re: Kelly Clarkson’s Feud With a Brooklyn Magic Shop…

OK, here’s a very silly but very big story: “Miss Independent” singer Kelly Clarkson is in a furious internet dispute with tiny Brooklyn magic shop the Art of Play over whether or not its staff was rude to her when she inquired about buying a certain singing bird sculpture. Seriously, look it up. Huge story . I’m here to say: I’m team Art of Play all the way. It sells incredible puzzles sourced from around the world, and I saw the best magic show of my life—by the incomparable David Williamson —in the hidden theater behind the bookshelf in the back. While I was there, I also happened to ask about the magic wind-up bird sculpture, which the owners show off before each performance. It’s by an artist named Bliss Kolb from Seattle. Being from Seattle myself and having a dad who loves clocks and other wind-up gizmos, I also, like Clarkson, wanted more details, and I will say the staff seemed mildly cagey. But I simply interpreted this as them maintaining an air of mystery. The bird in question is like the mascot for the store! And the entire wonder of the store is that it feels full of secrets!

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Art of Play (@artofplay)

A Random List of Culture’s ‘Free Thinkers’…

For some reason, for its 40th birthday, the Independent has dropped the “Independent’s Free Thinkers List,” featuring “people who have exhibited free thinking” during the paper’s lifetime. The 40 chosen Free Thinkers include artists Ai Weiwei (“changing the possibilities of politically engaged contemporary art“) and Tracey Emin (“helped make confession, vulnerability and autobiography legitimate subjects for contemporary art”). These picks do not exactly symbolize “radical free-thinking”; they are pretty familiar. The rest of the list’s grab bag includes the likes of Virgil Abloh , Richard Dawkins , Deng Xiaoping , Elon Musk , Shonda Rhimes , Margaret Thatcher , and Donald J. Trump . What a head-scratcher.

A Second Opinion on Mark Fisher…

The late theorist Mark Fisher , author of Capitalist Realism (2009), remains one of the major theory references in an art writing world that has largely replaced theory with attitude. Writer and researcher Rômulo Moraes has a scathing, attitude- and theory-filled dissent at his blog Ear Vortex . The one-line summary is this: Fisher was “a producer of false urgencies and chewed-up thought processes lifted and resized from the better work of others.” I happen to agree that Fisher’s cultural pessimism has outlived its sell-by date, reprocessed into the dull work of a commentator like W. David Marx in Blank Space (2025). To Moraes’s credit, the bulk of his essay is devoted to proposing thinkers he sees as better than Fisher.

Bad at Sports turned 21 with a tailgate party at the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago. Image courtesy Bad at Sports.

An Anniversary-of-Note for the Art-Pod-Sphere…

The OG art podcast, Chicago-based weekly Bad at Sports , celebrated 999 episodes at the beginning of this month, with a big live onstage conversation at the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago featuring New York mag’s critic, Jerry Saltz . That’s just one shy of 1,000 episodes! An accomplishment worth celebrating! I’ve been on B@S twice, and both times (episode # 767 , in 2021, and # 912 , last year), the chatty informal style let us get both weirder and more personal than almost anywhere else. The Saltz ep, which goes up online and on Lumpen Radio , will come out later in 2026. Congrats!

Something Not to Miss…

“ The Bowery: Devil’s Mile ” is an unexpected crowd-pleaser at the New Museum , not to be lost in the furor over Arthur Jafa , which opened at the same time (odd habit, that—almost guaranteeing things get lost in the mix). Surveying the long, long history of the Bowery as a creative site, the show serves as former New Museum director Lisa Phillips ’s final show, as if to put her legacy in context, and is co-curated by up-and-comer Thalia Stefaniuk . (At the press conference, Phillips affectionately compared their dynamic to the show Hacks ). Art highlights range from portraits of Bowery characters by Billy Sullivan and a suite of engaging sculptures by contemporary artist Brad Kahlhamer , whose studio is on the Bowery, to Jacob Riis ’s formative social documentary work How the Other Half Lives (1890) and Nan Goldin ’s incomparably moving The Ballad of Sexual Dependency (1985). But—surprisingly or unsurprisingly—the copious well-chosen non-art artifacts pack just as much punch, fleshing out the New York neighborhood’s history as a site of creative experimentation in the fullest popular sense. A civic-minded, serious, and seriously delightful exhibition.

The “Feejee Mermaid,” displayed in “The Bowery: Devil’s Mile.” Photo by Ben Davis.

“The Bowery: Devil’s Mile” 2026. Exhibition view: New Museum, New York. Courtesy New Museum. Photo: Dario Lasagni.

Works by Billy Sullivan and Bradley Kahlhamer in “The Bowery: Devil’s Mile.” Courtesy New Museum. Photo: Dario Lasagni.

article_text:
The Louvre temporarily closed Monday due to about 50 protesting arts and culture students, who blocked its glass pyramid entrance, Le Figaro reports. Their action comes on the one-year anniversary of the brazen jewelry heist at the same museum, and follows a massive, nationwide protest on Saturday against social inequality, particularly visible in public schools, which spiraled into clashes with police and riots. These continued to a lesser degree Sunday evening.

The unrest has come on the eve of Art Basel Paris this week, sparking concerns about how it will impact a week of art events throughout the city. It is still too early to know whether protests will continue in the coming days, but locals are hopeful that a school holiday will help calm tensions.

In response, Art Basel issued a statement Sunday reassuring visitors that “the fair is proceeding as planned,” and “additional security personnel have been deployed to patrol the perimeter of the fair 24 hours a day.” This should supplement what the fair described as existing, “extensive protocols in place,” to ensure “safety of all guests, exhibitors and staff, as well as the security of the artworks.”

These include anti-ram barriers around the Grand Palais, and “thorough security screening protocols” for visitors. The fair also noted it works with a private security company along with Paris police where necessary.

Meanwhile, over the weekend, most art openings continued as planned, despite the added difficulty of getting around town due to closed streets, subways, and skirmishes between police and protesters. Many bystanders found themselves caught in the smoke from burning street barricades and tear gas. In response, several sources said that many visitors to the city this week are hiring cars, and a few have canceled hotel reservations.

Some art spaces temporarily closed their doors. The opening of Stan Douglas ’s show Parallax at the Jeu de Paume on Sunday was canceled “out of precaution,” and because the surrounding Tuileries gardens were closed for the same reason, a museum spokesperson told ARTnews . Hauser & Wirth also closed their space in the 8th arrondissement on Saturday “as a precaution to protect the team, visitors and staff,” a representative said in an email.

At Marian Goodman Gallery in the Marais, where an exhibition opened with a new film by Bruce Nauman and Tacita Dean, most managed to make it “through the barricades,” despite breathing in tear gas to attend the opening dinner, where Dean thanked everyone for coming. Later that night, ARTnews saw adult male looters running out of shops on rue du Temple in the Marais, their arms full of merchandise.

Thousands of shops were looted in France on the sidelines and following protests that gathered over 500,000 people in city centers around the country, according to authorities. Public buildings, including a 19th-century town hall in Limoges, were badly burned, and nearly 2,400 people were arrested.

France’s interior minister admitted police had “lost control” of some areas and offered to resign. However, French President Emmanuel Macron refused his tender and has promised swift repercussions against looters, as well as a review of new security “operational methods.” Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu announced today that future curfews may be put in place where necessary, as soon as Monday night, to protect shops. More on those specifics is expected later today.

No damage was reportedly done to the Louvre, and protesters were not able to enter the glass pyramid. The museum’s website said that “due to student strikes, the museum is currently closed.” According to the AFP , the protesters at the Louvre, including students at art schools such as the associated École du Louvre, said they were angry at the violent response of police to protesters in recent weeks and wanted to show support for students and others demanding better conditions in public schools and the rising cost of living.

At the Sunday night opening of Jenny Holzer ’s exhibition at the Musée d’Orsay, titled “J’ai Vue” (I Saw), guests discussed how they had experienced the protests, as well as the timeliness of Holzer’s show, which directly addresses global conflict. (Holzer was unwell and could not attend in person.) Artist Kendalle Getty said that the process of mounting her new exhibition at ITEM IDEM gallery titled “ L’Identification Avec L’Autre ” (Identification with the Other), on rue Bleue in the 9th arrondissement, had been a challenge amid weeks of disruptions from ongoing student protests. Now, she also fears that her large-scale works made of mirrors, inspired by the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, could be at risk of damage by looters.

Shauna Torres, who installed and organized Getty’s exhibit, said she got stuck in tear gas on Saturday, but is trying to keep a positive outlook. “We’re living in history, and sometimes that smells like fires and tear gas and champagne, but I’m just happy to be here,” she said.

article_text:
La actriz de Verity reveló una tierna anécdota familiar y explicó por qué Lionel Messi es “un puente hacia tantas cosas maravillosas”.

Lionel Messi volvió a aparecer en una historia inesperada que llega desde Hollywood. Esta vez, el protagonista indirecto fue el hijo de Anne Hathaway , quien encontró en el capitán argentino la clave para romper el hielo y comenzar una nueva amistad.

La actriz contó la divertida anécdota durante una entrevista realizada en el marco de la promoción de Verity , el thriller psicológico que protagoniza junto a Dakota Johnson y Josh Hartnett .

La pregunta sobre el astro que cambió todo

Hathaway explicó que su hijo estaba conociendo a otro niño, pero ninguno de los dos encontraba la manera de comenzar una conversación. “Los chicos pueden ser tímidos alrededor de otros. Son solo niños y no saben de qué hablar”, contó la actriz al recordar la situación.

Fue entonces cuando decidió intervenir con una pregunta que, inesperadamente, funcionó a la perfección: “¿Te gusta Messi?” . La respuesta fue afirmativa. El otro niño dijo que sí y el hijo de Hathaway rápidamente se sumó: “Me encanta Messi” .

A partir de ese momento, todo cambió. Según relató la actriz, los dos chicos encontraron un punto en común y terminaron convirtiéndose en grandes amigos. Para Hathaway, la historia demuestra el enorme poder que tiene la figura del futbolista argentino incluso entre los más chicos.

¿Quién es quién en La Odisea de Christopher Nolan?

“ Es un puente hacia tantas cosas. Un puente para tantas cosas maravillosas ” , expresó la actriz al hablar del futbolista.

La actriz lo destacó como embajador

La anécdota surgió después de que Hathaway comenzara a hablar sobre su vínculo con la Argentina.

Durante la entrevista, la actriz recordó también su encuentro con Joaquín Furriel en Shanghái. Ambos coincidieron en 2024 durante un evento de Moncler, marca de lujo de la que son embajadores. En aquella oportunidad, Furriel había aprovechado para hablarle sobre la Argentina e incluso invitarla a conocer el país.

Cuando le preguntaron si el actor había hecho un buen trabajo promocionando nuestro país, Hathaway respondió que la Argentina tiene “tantos embajadores increíbles”. Entre ellos mencionó al polista Nacho Figueras y, naturalmente, al fútbol argentino. “Tienen a su equipo de fútbol entero. Tienen a Messi” , destacó la actriz.

La referencia al rosarino derivó entonces en la particular historia de su hijo, que terminó demostrando de una manera muy sencilla el alcance internacional de la figura del capitán argentino.

También habló de la Argentina

No es la primera vez que Hathaway tiene un acercamiento público con la cultura argentina y latinoamericana.

Durante la promoción de El diablo viste a la moda 2 , la actriz protagonizó junto a Meryl Streep un divertido momento en México al bailar Cómo te voy a olvidar , uno de los grandes clásicos de Los Ángeles Azules.

Ahora, con Verity como nuevo proyecto, volvió a referirse a la Argentina y a algunas de sus figuras más reconocidas. En la misma entrevista, Dakota Johnson también habló de Buenos Aires y contó que visitó la ciudad en varias oportunidades. Josh Hartnett , en cambio, reconoció que todavía no conoce el país, aunque manifestó sus ganas de hacerlo.
